newsitem.title: USA: Relaxed, confident Clinton stumps in central Florida.
newsitem.headline: Relaxed, confident Clinton stumps in central Florida.

text.p: With polls showing him pulling away from Republican rival Bob Dole, President Bill Clinton took time for golf on Wednesday before taking a sunny new message to voters -- deadbeat parents are shaping up.
Speaking at a midday rally at this oceanfront city in central Florida, Clinton highlighted a government report showing that child support payments have risen 50 percent over the last four years.

"We're going to keep going until we raise child support more and more and more. We're going to move hundreds of thousands of people off welfare by making sure that the parents do what they ought to do -- take responsibility for their children and their future," he told a cheering crowd gathered under a sunny sky as palm trees shimmered in the Indian River lagoon behind him.

Child support enforcement is primarily a local issue more appropriate in campaigns for sheriff than president, but White House spokesman Mike McCurry said it would be a key element in successfully implementing a tough new welfare law that Clinton signed in August. Making that law work will be a "major challenge" for whoever leads the United States in the next four years, McCurry said.
Clinton flew to Daytona Beach after a stop in Miami and an early morning round of golf. He told reporters he played nine holes in 43 strokes and called his game "mediocre."

Perhaps the most striking aspect of Clinton's visit to Florida was that it showed his appeal in a state that is traditionally hostile to Democratic presidential candidates. He planned forays into normally Republican Alabama, Louisiana and Georgia later this week.
A recent Tampa Tribune poll showed Clinton with a narrow 47-44 lead over Dole for Florida's 25 electoral votes -- just under 10 percent of the 270 electoral votes needed to win the presidency.

Doug Sosnik, a White House political strategist, said Clinton was polling about 41 percent of the Cuban-American vote, "and the conventional wisdom is if a Democrat gets 30 percent of that vote, we carry the state."
Dole was campaigning in conservative northwest Florida on Wednesday, an area that a Republican would normally have locked up at this point in the presidential race.

Nationally, Clinton's lead over Dole continued to strengthen with less than two weeks to go before the Nov. 5 election. A daily tracking poll sponsored by Reuters showed Clinton ahead of his Republican opponent by 11.7 percent on Wednesday, a slight gain from Tuesday's poll.

Other Reuters polls showed Clinton with commanding double-digit leads in the two key states of Michigan and Ohio, and a Los Angeles Times poll published on Wednesday showed Clinton with a 20 percentage point lead in California.

Dole decided last week to concentrate many of his remaining resources on California in a make-or-break effort to overtake Clinton after a poll by another organisation said he had cut the president's lead in the state to 10 points.

In another campaign-related development, McCurry said Clinton was sending a personal note to former first lady Nancy Reagan, who complained about a Clinton campaign ad that included footage of March, 1981 assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan.

Clinton planned to tell Mrs. Reagan that the ad, which features former Reagan press secretary James Brady, is scheduled to go off the air within the next day or so and that "her views will be taken into consideration" if it it used again after that, the White House spokesman said.
